checks.prompt: You prune 90% of a linear layer's weights to zero with unstructured magnitude pruning and benchmark it on a standard GPU with a normal dense matmul. What speedup should you expect?
options: Essentially none — the matrix has the same shape and the dense kernel does the same work
About 10×, matching the fraction of weights removed
About 2×, the practical ceiling for sparse execution
Somewhat slower than dense, because the zeros must be skipped at runtime
checks.explanation: This is the notebook's central measurement: a 90%-sparse matrix of unchanged shape benchmarks at 1.00× against dense, while a structurally pruned matrix of 1/10 the rows benchmarks over 7×. A dense kernel has no idea the zeros are there. Sparsity percentage is not a performance number.

checks.prompt: In the tree analogy, why does removing scattered twigs preserve accuracy better than cutting a whole branch, even at the same total mass removed?
options: Unstructured pruning can choose the least important individual weights anywhere, while structured pruning must remove a whole group including the important weights inside it
Scattered removal is spread across more layers, so the damage per layer is lower
Whole branches carry the gradient signal, while twigs only carry forward activations
Structured pruning removes weights at random, whereas unstructured pruning ranks them by magnitude
checks.explanation: Unstructured pruning has complete freedom of choice, so at a given sparsity it can always find a lower-error solution than a method constrained to remove entire rows or channels. That freedom is exactly what makes it invisible to dense hardware — the shape never changes.

checks.prompt: Explain what the 2:4 sparsity pattern is, why it exists at all given that unstructured pruning achieves lower error at the same 50% sparsity, and what hardware condition must hold for it to be worth using.
checks.expected: A correct answer must state that 2:4 means exactly two of every contiguous group of four weights are zero, fixing sparsity at 50% by construction. It must explain that the constraint exists because NVIDIA sparse tensor cores (Ampere and later) can execute this specific pattern at roughly 2× dense throughput, whereas unstructured sparsity yields no speedup on dense hardware — so 2:4 trades a modest amount of extra approximation error for a real wall-clock win. It must note the hardware condition: on pre-Ampere hardware (or without kernel support) 2:4 is pure accuracy loss for no benefit.
checks.explanation: 2:4 is the compromise the silicon was designed around: scattered zeros, but with a rule about how they may scatter, so the hardware can skip them.

checks.prompt: Write `prune_2of4(weights)` which takes a flat list of floats whose length is a multiple of 4 and returns a new list where, in each contiguous group of 4, the two entries with the smallest absolute value are replaced by 0.0 and the other two are unchanged. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Note the last assertion: the input list must not be mutated. Selecting by absolute value is what makes this magnitude pruning; the grouping is what makes it 2:4.

checks.prompt: You apply global magnitude pruning at 80% across a network and one layer comes back 100% zero. What happened, and what is the standard fix?
options: That layer's weights are on a much smaller scale than the rest, so the global threshold consumed all of them — apply a per-layer sparsity floor
The layer was already redundant and can safely be deleted from the network entirely
Global pruning always removes whole layers by design; use iterative pruning instead to avoid it
The magnitude criterion cannot handle negative weights, so a layer with mostly negative weights is wiped out
checks.explanation: Global ranking pools weights across layers, so a layer whose weights are uniformly small in absolute terms looks entirely unimportant even when it is doing essential work. This is exactly what happens in the notebook's Example 1. Real recipes use global ranking with a per-layer floor.

checks.prompt: Describe the comparison you must run before concluding that pruning a large model to 50% was worthwhile, and explain why the obvious comparison is misleading.
checks.expected: A correct answer must say that the pruned model should be compared against a DENSE model of the same final size (same parameter count or same latency), not against the original unpruned model. The obvious comparison — pruned versus original — only tells you how much accuracy you lost, not whether pruning was the right way to reach that size; very often simply training the smaller dense model outright matches or beats the pruned one, which is a central lesson of the lottery-ticket literature. Mentioning that you must also measure latency rather than sparsity percentage is a plus.
checks.explanation: The baseline that matters is the alternative you would otherwise have shipped, which is a smaller dense model — not the model you started with.
